lead: A processor spends most of its silicon on arithmetic and on memory. This unit builds the adder, the multiplier, the decoder, the latch and the memory cell from CMOS gates, and shows where the delay and the area go. After it you can size an adder for a target clock, read a multiplier array, and choose SRAM, DRAM or ROM for a given job.
about: The unit starts at the adder. Chapter 4.1 builds the full adder, shows why the ripple carry is slow, and how carry look-ahead removes the wait. Chapter 4.2 trades area for speed with carry select, carry save and carry skip. Chapter 4.3 arranges adders into a 2-D array to multiply, including the signed Baugh-Wooley form. Chapter 4.4 compresses the partial products with a Wallace tree and halves their count with Booth recoding. Chapter 4.5 moves to the routing blocks: decoders, multiplexers and comparators. Chapter 4.6 stores one bit reliably with static and dynamic latches, master-slave registers and their timing rules. Chapter 4.7 puts those cells into rows and columns to build SRAM, DRAM and ROM. Each chapter feeds the next: adders to multipliers, decoders and registers to memory.

chapters.idea: A full adder adds three bits; a wide adder is many of them, and the only real design question is how fast the carry reaches the last bit.
chapters.depth: Half adder (S = a⊕b, C = a·b) and full adder (S = a⊕b⊕c, C = a·b + c·(a⊕b)) with truth tables. The transistor-level standard adder cell — some syllabi call it the mirror adder, 28 transistors. Ripple carry adder: n full adders in a row, worst-case carry path of 2n gate delays, and the sum arriving one XOR delay later. Generate g_i = a_i·b_i and propagate p_i = a_i⊕b_i; warn that some texts define p_i = a_i + b_i, so state your choice. Carry recurrence c_{i+1} = g_i + p_i·c_i, expanded by hand for 4 bits, then the carry look-ahead generator block (also called LCU or look-ahead carry unit). Group generate and group propagate for wider adders. Cost and delay comparison. Subtraction with c0 = 1 and an XOR on each B bit.

figure.title: Two paths to the last sum bit
figure.aria: The ripple path goes from full adder to sum bit through every stage, while the look-ahead block computes all carries in parallel.

chapters.example: Add a = 1011 (11) and b = 0110 (6) with a 4-bit carry look-ahead adder, c0 = 0. g_i = a_i·b_i gives g3 g2 g1 g0 = 0100. p_i = a_i⊕b_i gives p3 p2 p1 p0 = 1011. Carries: c1 = g0 + p0·c0 = 0, c2 = g1 + p1·c1 = 1, c3 = g2 + p2·c2 = 1, c4 = g3 + p3·c3 = 1. Sums s_i = p_i⊕c_i: s0 = 1, s1 = 0, s2 = 0, s3 = 0. Result c4 s3 s2 s1 s0 = 10001 = 17, and 11 + 6 = 17.
chapters.trap: Using OR instead of XOR for propagate, and forgetting that each sum bit needs one more XOR after its carry arrives. Fix your definition of p on paper before writing any formula.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for the CMOS gates that realise AND, OR and XOR; basic digital logic for the half and full adder.
chapters.leave: Transistor sizing, logical effort and gate power to Unit 3; adder test patterns to Unit 6; pipelining the adder to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: When the carry chain is the bottleneck you compute both possible answers and select, save the carry for later, or skip over a block that only propagates.
chapters.depth: Carry skip (also called carry bypass): block propagate P = p_m·…·p_n, a multiplexer that passes the incoming carry across the block when P = 1, and the square-root block size that minimises delay. Carry select: two ripple adders per block, one with c_in = 0 and one with c_in = 1, a multiplexer on each sum bit, then the square-root layout that duplicates only the high blocks. Area counted in full adders. Carry save adder: a row of full adders used as a 3:2 compressor, producing a sum vector S and a carry vector C with no carry propagation at all, plus a final carry propagate adder. Names to recognise: CSL, CSA, CSK.

figure.title: Carry select adder
figure.aria: Two ripple adders run in parallel with different carry inputs and a multiplexer keeps the correct result.

chapters.example: Add a = 1011 (11), b = 0110 (6) and c = 0101 (5) with one row of carry save adders. Column 0: 1+0+1 = 2, so s0 = 0 and carry into column 1 is 1. Column 1: 1+1+0 = 2, so s1 = 0 and carry is 1. Column 2: 0+1+1 = 2, so s2 = 0 and carry is 1. Column 3: 1+0+0 = 1, so s3 = 1 and the carry out is 0. Sum vector S = 1000 (8). Carry vector C = 0111 shifted one place left = 1110 (14). Final add gives 8 + 14 = 22 = 11 + 6 + 5.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to shift the carry vector left by one bit before the final add, and expecting a carry save adder to produce a finished sum on its own.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for the full adder and for g and p.
chapters.leave: Choice of final carry propagate adder to Chapter 4.1; use of the compressor inside multipliers to Chapter 4.4.

chapters.idea: A multiplier array forms all partial products at once with AND gates and adds them at fixed positions, so the product is ready after one long diagonal carry ripple.
chapters.depth: Unsigned multiplication as shift and add; n partial products of n bits. The 4×4 array needs n² AND gates and n(n−1) full adders, carries run diagonally, and the critical path reaches the last row. Braun multiplier: the plain unsigned array with no correction terms, its regular layout and its delay. Baugh-Wooley: two's complement array, sign-bit rows inverted, correction constants (two 1s) added at fixed positions, and why it beats sign-extension or a separate sign-fix stage. Gate counts and delay. Some syllabi ask only for the block diagram and the partial product array of these two.

figure.title: 4×4 Braun array, a = 1101
figure.aria: Each row is the multiplicand gated by one bit of the multiplier, and the row gated by b2 equals zero so it adds nothing.

chapters.example: Multiply a = 1101 (13) by b = 1011 (11) on a 4×4 Braun array. Partial products: b0 = 1 gives 1101; b1 = 1 gives 1101 shifted one place = 11010 (26); b2 = 0 gives 0000; b3 = 1 gives 1101 shifted three places = 1101000 (104). Sum = 13 + 26 + 0 + 104 = 143 = 10001111. Check: 13 × 11 = 143.
chapters.trap: In Baugh-Wooley, dropping the correction constants or inverting the wrong row; in Braun, adding the partial products without their shifts.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.1 and 4.2 for the full adder and the carry save idea.
chapters.leave: Fast reduction of the rows to Chapter 4.4; physical layout of the array to Unit 2; pipelining to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A Wallace tree attacks the delay of summing many rows with a tree of 3:2 counters, while Booth attacks the number of rows by recoding the multiplier into signed digits.
chapters.depth: Wallace tree: the carry save adder as a 3:2 counter, rows reduced in parallel at every level, depth growing like the log of the row count, irregular wiring, one final carry propagate adder. Counting exercise: 8 rows become 6, then 4, then 3, then 2. Dadda tree mentioned only as the variant that pushes counters as late as possible. Booth radix-2: the extra bit q−1 = 0, the recoding table for the pair (q_i, q−1): 00 gives 0, 01 gives +M, 10 gives −M, 11 gives 0, and an arithmetic right shift. Radix-4 modified Booth: digits from −2 to +2 and the 3M multiple it needs. Booth's gains: fewer partial products and no separate sign handling.

figure.aria: Eight partial product rows are reduced by carry save adders level by level until two rows remain for the final adder.

chapters.example: Recode Q = 1101 with q−1 = 0 for a Booth multiplier with M = 0110 (+6). Pairs from the LSB: (q0, q−1) = (1,0) gives −M; (q1, q0) = (0,1) gives +M; (q2, q1) = (1,0) gives −M; (q3, q2) = (1,1) gives 0. The digits −1, +1, −1, 0 with weights 1, 2, 4, 8 give −1 + 2 − 4 + 0 = −3, which is right because 1101 in two's complement is −3. Product = 6 × (−3) = −18 = 11101110 in 8 bits.
chapters.trap: Booth: forgetting the extra bit q−1 = 0 and using a logical shift instead of an arithmetic shift. Wallace: counting the final carry propagate adder as one more reduction level.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for the 3:2 compressor and Chapter 4.3 for the partial product rows.
chapters.leave: Array layout and design-rule checks to Unit 2; multiplier test patterns to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A decoder turns a code into one active line, a multiplexer turns many lines into one, and a comparator turns two words into a decision.
chapters.depth: n-to-2ⁿ decoder: AND plane with inverters, active-high and active-low outputs, the decoder as a minterm generator, larger decoders built from smaller ones using an enable input, and the decoder as a memory row driver. Multiplexer: 2:1 from pass transistors and transmission gates (cross-reference Unit 3), mux tree for 4:1 and 8:1, the mux as a logic element by Shannon expansion, tristate outputs. Comparator: 1-bit equality with XNOR, n-bit equality as an AND tree, the magnitude cell with (A>B), (A<B), (A=B) and the iterative chain that settles the answer from the MSB down. Gate-level delay of each block.

figure.title: Three routing blocks
figure.aria: The same input bits feed a decoder, a multiplexer and a comparator, and each block produces its own result.

chapters.example: Implement f(A,B,C) = Σm(1,2,5,7). With a 3-to-8 decoder and one OR gate, tie outputs Y1, Y2, Y5, Y7 to the OR. With an 8:1 multiplexer, use A, B, C as select lines and set the data inputs D0 to D7 = 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1. Next compare A = 1011 (11) with B = 1010 (10): reading from the MSB, the first three bit pairs are equal and the last pair is 1 against 0, so the last cell sets A > B.
chapters.trap: Reading an active-low decoder output as active-high, and letting a comparator decide from the LSB end instead of the MSB end.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for pass transistor and transmission gate multiplexers; Chapter 4.1 for the XOR used in equality.
chapters.leave: Tristate and pass transistor detail to Unit 3; memory row decoders to Chapter 4.7; decoded control in a state machine to another unit.

chapters.idea: A latch stores a bit in a feedback loop that is open for part of the clock, and two latches in series make an edge-triggered register.
chapters.depth: Cross-coupled NOR and NAND SR latch; gated D latch, transparent when the clock is high or low; master-slave D flip-flop built from two latches on two clock phases, and why edge triggering is needed. Timing terms defined with symbols: setup time t_su, hold time t_h, clock-to-Q delay t_cq, aperture, and the two checks — setup on the longest path, hold on the shortest path. Static versus dynamic storage: charge held on a gate capacitance, leakage, and the minimum clock rate a dynamic latch needs. Transmission-gate latch. Registers as n flip-flops in parallel, with enable, reset and shift versions. Two-phase non-overlapping clocking: only a few universities teach the detail.

figure.aria: The latch follows the input whenever the clock is high, while the register output changes only at the clock edges.

chapters.example: A path between two registers has clock-to-Q t_cq = 0.3 ns, combinational delay t_comb = 1.2 ns, setup time t_su = 0.15 ns, hold time t_h = 0.10 ns and clock period T = 2 ns. Setup slack = T − t_cq − t_comb − t_su = 2 − 0.3 − 1.2 − 0.15 = 0.35 ns, which is ≥ 0, so setup passes. Hold check: t_cq + t_comb = 1.5 ns ≥ 0.10 ns, so hold passes. The shortest clock period is 0.3 + 1.2 + 0.15 = 1.65 ns, so the maximum frequency is about 606 MHz.
chapters.trap: Calling a latch edge-triggered, and checking only setup while ignoring the hold check on the short path.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for the transmission gate and for the delay of the inverter pair inside the storage loop.
chapters.leave: Clock distribution and clock power to Unit 3; scan flip-flops to Unit 6; register transfer level coding to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A memory is a two-dimensional array of identical cells: the row decoder picks one word, the cells put their bits on the bitlines, and a sense amplifier decides each bit.
chapters.depth: Array organisation, address bits split into row and column, wordline and bitline, row decoder from Chapter 4.5, column multiplexer, sense amplifier, write driver, and the difference between access time and cycle time. 6T SRAM cell: two cross-coupled inverters plus two access transistors, read and write operation, read disturb and the cell ratio described in words only. 1T1C DRAM cell: charge storage, charge sharing with the bitline, destructive read and restore, refresh and the maximum time between accesses, density advantage. ROM: mask ROM with one transistor per bit, then PROM, EPROM, EEPROM and flash in one line each. Comparison of density, speed, volatility, refresh and standby power.

figure.title: 4×4 memory array
figure.aria: One wordline is driven high by the row decoder and its four cells place their bits on the bitlines.

chapters.example: A 256 Kbit SRAM is built as 1024 words × 256 bits. Address bits = log₂ 1024 = 10, so the row decoder is a 10-to-1024 decoder. Cells = 1024 × 256 = 262144 = 2^18, which is 256 K. A DRAM with 4096 rows must refresh every row within 64 ms: 4096 ÷ 64 ms = 64 rows per ms, that is one row every 15.6 µs.
chapters.trap: Mixing up access time with cycle time, and forgetting that a DRAM read destroys the stored charge and must be written back.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.5 for decoders and multiplexers, Chapter 4.6 for the storage loop and timing rules.
chapters.leave: Memory fault models and March tests to Unit 6; sense amplifier analog design to an analog course; cache policy to computer architecture.
